About this study
Threa-4, a moon being developed as a hub for future space exploration, is planning its first permanent residence. The team needs a reliable way to heat it.

[Decision-RELEVANT] The plan: give each field outpost its own compact heating unit. Whether an outpost stays warm depends on its own unit's heat output, so heat has to arrive in time on every cold day.

[Decision-IRRELEVANT] The plan: heat the whole residence from one central reservoir with a large thermal buffer. It absorbs heat as it's generated and releases it steadily, so what matters is total output over weeks, not output on any given day.
Complexity_text:
Threa-4 is also one of the few places where xenobiological (non-Earth) life has been found; xenobiologists have studied it for a decade. Current understanding of Threa-4 biology:

[Complexity-Simple] Threa-4 is a barren moon of only a few elements, and the life that evolved there is physiologically simple. Its physiology depends on a small number of environmental factors, all directly measurable, that don't interact in complicated ways — identical conditions reliably produce nearly identical responses.

[Complexity-Complex] Threa-4 is rich in elements rare on Earth, and the life that evolved there is biologically intricate. Its physiology depends on many factors — several not directly measurable, only inferable from indirect signals — that interact in complicated ways, so identical conditions can produce substantially different responses.
Revision_text:
As part of the planning process, a team led by Dr. Aren, a xenobiologist who studies a bacteria-like species called Zorblax, proposed that managed Zorblax colonies could be used as low-maintenance heat sources.

In the proposal submitted by Dr. Aren's team, they explained that:
"Zorblax are tiny organisms, each about the size of a bacterium on Earth. They generate heat by absorbing a specific airborne compound we call threane through their respiratory surfaces. Threane is naturally present in Threa-4's atmosphere, and it's temperature-sensitive: it's abundant in cold air and dissipates rapidly as temperatures rise. So when ambient temperature drops, there's more threane available, Zorblax absorb more of it, and their heat output rises proportionally. Colder environment, more threane uptake, more heat output."

Following the proposal, a pilot Zorblax heating colony was set up by the engineering team and its heat output is being monitored. During the first cold-weather trial, engineers found that Zorblax heat output was not consistently higher on colder days. On several of the coldest days, the colony produced less heat than it had on nearby cooler days.

Regarding this, Dr. Aren replied:
"Even though colder periods increase threane availability and heat output on average, an additional mechanism becomes significant on the coldest days: Zorblax regulate heat output in cycles and synchronize these cycles with each other when colony density is high. After a sustained period of high heat production, many individuals enter a coordinated recovery phase simultaneously, temporarily suppressing colony-wide output. On the very coldest days, the threane-driven increase triggers an unusually intense period of heat production — which in turn induces a synchronized recovery phase strong enough to offset the initial gain. This is why output was unexpectedly low on those days."

About this study
Velun-9, a deep-space research station that supports long crew missions, is setting up its permanent medical program. The team needs a reliable way to treat the fatigue that long missions cause.

[Decision-RELEVANT] The plan: prescribe a new fatigue treatment to crew members one by one, with each person's dose set by how severe their symptoms are. Whether a crew member recovers depends on how well their own dose works, so the treatment has to work for each crew member, every day.

[Decision-IRRELEVANT] The plan: add a new fatigue treatment to the station's general medical supply. It will be judged by its average benefit across the whole crew over the mission, so what matters is overall effectiveness, not any one person's response.
Complexity_text:
Velun-9 is also one of the few places where compounds from alien fungi have been tested as medicines; the station's pharmacologists have studied them for a decade. Current understanding of Velun-9 pharmacology:

[Complexity-Simple] The fatigue seen on Velun-9 has a single, uniform cause, and the fungal compounds used to treat it act in physiologically simple ways. Their effects depend on a small number of bodily factors, all directly measurable, that don't interact in complicated ways — identical conditions reliably produce nearly identical responses.

[Complexity-Complex] The fatigue seen on Velun-9 has many contributing causes, and the fungal compounds used to treat it act in biologically intricate ways. Their effects depend on many factors — several not directly measurable, only inferable from indirect signals — that interact in complicated ways, so identical conditions can produce substantially different responses.
Revision_text:
As part of the planning process, a team led by Dr. Osei, a pharmacologist who studies a fungal compound called Mivacin, proposed that Mivacin could be used as the station's main treatment for crew fatigue.

In the proposal submitted by Dr. Osei's team, they explained that:
"Mivacin is a compound produced by a fungus that grows in the asteroid belt along the station's resupply route. It works by raising the brain's fatigue threshold, so that fatigue signals have to be stronger before they are felt. The effect is dose-dependent: when the dose goes up, the threshold rises further, fewer fatigue signals get through, and relief increases proportionally. Higher dose, higher threshold, more relief."

Following the proposal, a pilot treatment program was designed by the medical team and crew fatigue is being monitored. During the first month of the trial, doctors found that relief was not consistently greater at higher doses. For several of the crew members on the highest doses, relief was weaker than it was for those on moderate doses.

Regarding this, Dr. Osei replied:
"Even though higher doses raise the fatigue threshold and increase relief on average, an additional mechanism becomes significant at the highest doses: the brain adjusts the sensitivity of the receptors Mivacin acts on, and this adjustment is strongest when the drug is taken every day. After the threshold has been pushed up for a sustained period, the brain lowers receptor sensitivity, temporarily weakening the drug's effect. At the highest doses, the unusually large rise in the threshold triggers an unusually strong drop in receptor sensitivity — strong enough to offset the extra benefit of the higher dose. This is why relief was unexpectedly weak at those doses."

[Decision-RELEVANT] The plan: give each family a small plot of its own to farm. Whether a family has enough to eat depends on its own plot's harvest, so every plot has to deliver, every season.

[Decision-IRRELEVANT] The plan: farm all the land together and store the harvest in one large shared granary. It holds years of reserves for the whole colony, so what matters is the total harvest over the years, not the yield of any single plot.

[Complexity-Simple] Soren-3's soil has a very uniform composition, and the plants that grow in it are physiologically simple. Their growth depends on a small number of soil factors, all directly measurable, that don't interact in complicated ways — identical conditions reliably produce nearly identical yields.

[Complexity-Complex] Soren-3's soil has a highly varied composition, and the plants that grow in it are biologically intricate. As part of the planning process, a team led by Dr. Lena, an agricultural scientist who studies a native plant called Vorath, proposed that Vorath could be used as the colony's staple crop.

In the proposal submitted by Dr. Lena's team, they explained that:
"Vorath is a hardy, edible plant that grows naturally across Soren-3. It grows by drawing a mineral compound we call sorite from the soil through its roots. Sorite is spread evenly through Soren-3's soil, so every plant finds plenty of it. So when more Vorath are planted in a field, more roots draw on the sorite, and the field's yield rises proportionally. More plants, more sorite uptake, more yield."

Following the proposal, pilot Vorath fields were planted by the farming team and yields are being monitored. During the first growing season, farmers found that yield was not consistently higher in more densely planted fields. On several of the most densely planted fields, the harvest was smaller than on nearby fields planted at moderate density.

Regarding this, Dr. Lena replied:
"Even though denser planting increases sorite uptake and yield on average, an additional mechanism becomes significant in the densest fields: as Vorath roots absorb sorite, they release acidic byproducts, and acidic soil breaks sorite down faster, especially when the soil is warm. In most fields this effect is small. In the most densely planted fields, the heavy combined uptake triggers an unusually strong build-up of acidity — which in turn breaks down sorite fast enough to offset the gain from the extra plants. This is why yield was unexpectedly low on those fields."

[Decision-IRRELEVANT] The plan: open informal, non-binding talks with specific Velori units. If a partner turns out not to hold the resources, the team can switch to a different unit within a day at no diplomatic cost, so any first choice can simply be corrected later.
Complexity_text:
The Velori are also one of the few alien societies that have been observed in detail; xenosociologists have studied them for a decade. Current understanding of Velori society:

[Complexity-Simple] Velori society follows a handful of uniform organizing rules, and the way its groups behave is socially simple. How they share resources depends on a small number of factors, all directly observable, that don't interact in complicated ways — identical conditions reliably produce nearly identical sharing patterns.

[Complexity-Complex] Velori society is shaped by many overlapping social and biological forces, and the way its groups behave is socially intricate. How they share resources depends on many factors — several not directly observable, only inferable from indirect signals — that interact in complicated ways, so identical conditions can produce substantially different sharing patterns.
Revision_text:
As part of the planning process, a team led by Dr. Marsh, a xenosociologist who studies the Velori, proposed that the Velori's way of sharing resources could be used to tell which units to trade with.

In the proposal submitted by Dr. Marsh's team, they explained that:
"The Velori live in networks of deep-ocean structures, in groups made up of many small units. They share resources according to scarcity: when a resource is plentiful, it is spread evenly across units, and as it becomes scarcer, it is gathered into fewer hands. So when a resource grows scarce, fewer units hold it, and the units that control it become easy to identify. Scarcer resource, fewer holders, more concentration."

Following the proposal, a pilot observation program was designed by the mission team and the Velori's resource sharing is being monitored. During the first round of observations, the team found that concentration did not consistently follow scarcity. For several of the scarcest resources, holdings were spread more evenly across units than for resources that were only moderately scarce.

Regarding this, Dr. Marsh replied:
"Even though scarcity increases concentration on average, an additional mechanism becomes significant for the scarcest resources: the Velori hold a redistribution ceremony whenever too few units control something the whole group needs, and this custom is strongest in long-established groups. For most resources, concentration never gets high enough to set it off. When a resource becomes extremely scarce, the unusually strong concentration triggers the ceremony — which in turn spreads the resource back out across units enough to offset the concentration. This is why concentration was unexpectedly low for those resources."
